concepts.title: Molecular Nature of Matter
concepts.definition: All matter is built from molecules -- atoms bound into groups -- with gaps between them far larger than the molecules themselves in gases. Avogadro's hypothesis that equal volumes of gas at the same conditions hold equal molecule counts fixes the counting unit: one mole contains 6.02 x 10^23 molecules.
concepts.key_idea: Behaviour of matter follows from molecule counts and gaps -- one mole is always 6.02e23 molecules regardless of the substance.
concepts.textbook_ref: keph205.txt lines 30-120 (sections 12.1, 12.2 molecular nature of matter, Dalton's atomic hypothesis, Avogadro's law and number)
question_patterns: state Avogadro's law and the value of Avogadro's number
in class 11 kinetic theory: how many molecules does one mole of any gas contain
find the number of molecules in the given mass of a substance
why did early scientists doubt the atomic hypothesis
what evidence supports the molecular picture of matter
relate moles mass and molecular mass in a counting problem

solution_steps.explain: Divide the sample's mass by its molecular mass to get the number of moles.
Multiplying moles by 6.02e23 gives the molecule count.
Equal volumes of different gases at the same temperature and pressure carry equal molecule numbers, which is why molar volumes match.

concepts.title: Gas Laws and the Ideal Gas Equation
concepts.definition: Dilute gases obey simple patterns: Boyle's law fixes pressure times volume at one temperature, Charles's law fixes volume over temperature at one pressure, and combining them with the amount of gas gives the ideal gas equation, pressure times volume equal to the number of moles times R times absolute temperature.
concepts.key_idea: pV = n R T packs Boyle and Charles into one state equation for any dilute gas.
concepts.textbook_ref: keph205.txt lines 121-260 (section 12.3 behaviour of gases, Boyle's law, Charles's law, pressure law, ideal gas equation, dew and humidity aside)
question_patterns: state Boyle's law and Charles's law with their conditions

a gas is compressed at constant temperature, find the new pressure
what is the value and meaning of the universal gas constant
combine the gas laws into the single ideal gas equation
find the volume of one mole of gas at standard temperature and pressure

solution_steps.action: multiply moles by R and temperature
solution_steps.explain: The right side n R T equals pressure times volume for an ideal gas.

concepts.title: Pressure of an Ideal Gas from Molecular Motion
concepts.definition: Gas pressure is the drumbeat of countless molecular impacts on the walls. Counting the collisions with momentum change per hit yields the kinetic theory result: pressure equals one third the product of the molecular number density and the mean squared molecular speed -- the square average of the speeds in the distribution.
concepts.key_idea: Pressure is molecular momentum delivered per second per area -- one third of density times mean square speed.
concepts.textbook_ref: keph205.txt lines 261-400 (section 12.4 kinetic theory of an ideal gas, pressure of an ideal gas, rms speed, assumptions of the theory)
question_patterns: derive the expression for the pressure of an ideal gas using kinetic theory
in class 11 kinetic theory: what is the rms speed and why is the square of it used
relate pressure to the mean square molecular speed
state the assumptions behind the kinetic theory of gases
why do faster molecules raise the pressure of a gas
connect the average kinetic energy of molecules to the gas temperature

solution_steps.explain: A molecule bouncing off a wall reverses one momentum component, delivering a fixed impulse per hit.
Averaging over random directions leaves one third of the mean squared speed contributing to each wall.
Pressure equals one third of mass density times the mean square speed, and temperature is proportional to that mean square speed.

concepts.title: RMS Speed of Gas Molecules
concepts.definition: Equating the kinetic theory pressure to the ideal gas law exposes the typical molecular speed: the root mean square speed equals the square root of three times the universal gas constant times absolute temperature, all over the molar mass. Light molecules therefore outrun heavy ones at the same temperature.
concepts.key_idea: Root of 3RT over M -- hydrogen molecules sprint about four times faster than oxygen at the same temperature.
concepts.textbook_ref: keph205.txt lines 330-400 (section 12.4 rms speed expression, dependence on molar mass and temperature)
question_patterns: find the rms speed of the given gas at the given temperature
in class 11 kinetic theory: how does rms speed depend on molar mass
compare the rms speeds of two gases at the same temperature
at what temperature does a gas molecule reach the given rms speed
why is the rms speed used rather than the simple average speed
estimate the typical molecular speed of air at room temperature

solution_steps.action: form the ratio under the root
solution_steps.explain: Multiply three, the gas constant and the temperature, then divide by the molar mass in kilograms per mole.
The root gives the root mean square molecular speed.

concepts.title: Law of Equipartition of Energy
concepts.definition: In thermal equilibrium every independent way a molecule can store energy -- each degree of freedom -- carries the same average energy, one half of Boltzmann's constant times temperature. A monatomic molecule with three translational degrees holds 3/2 kT; adding rotational degrees raises the share accordingly.
concepts.key_idea: Energy splits equally among available degrees of freedom -- half kT each, no favourites.
concepts.textbook_ref: keph205.txt lines 401-500 (section 12.5 law of equipartition of energy, degrees of freedom, monatomic and diatomic molecules, vibrational modes)
question_patterns: state the law of equipartition of energy
in class 11 kinetic theory: how many degrees of freedom does a diatomic molecule have
find the average energy of a monatomic molecule at the given temperature
why does each degree of freedom carry half kT
how do rotational modes change the energy share of a molecule
apply equipartition to count the total energy of a mole of gas

solution_steps.explain: Translation gives three always; rotations add two for linear diatomic molecules (three for nonlinear), and vibration adds more at high temperature.
Each degree of freedom stores half kT on average by the equipartition law.
Multiplying degrees of freedom by half kT gives the mean energy per molecule; scaling by Avogadro's number gives the molar internal energy.

concepts.title: Specific Heats of Gases from Equipartition
concepts.definition: Equipartition predicts molar specific heats directly: a monatomic gas needs 3/2 R to raise its temperature at constant volume, a diatomic gas 5/2 R once rotations join in. The predicted Cp minus Cv equals R in each case, matching Mayer's relation and explaining why gases differ in heat capacity by their molecular structure.
concepts.key_idea: Count the degrees of freedom, multiply by R over two -- that is the constant-volume molar specific heat.
concepts.textbook_ref: keph205.txt lines 480-560 (section 12.6 specific heat capacity of monatomic diatomic and polyatomic gases, agreement with experiment)
question_patterns: predict the molar specific heat of a monatomic gas at constant volume
in class 11 kinetic theory: why is Cv of a diatomic gas larger than that of a monatomic gas
verify Mayer's relation for the given gas using predicted heats
what happens to the specific heat when vibrational modes wake up
compute gamma for a diatomic gas from equipartition
relate the internal energy of a mole of gas to its Cv

solution_steps.explain: Monatomic: three translational degrees. Diatomic: five below the vibration turn-on temperature.
Cv equals degrees of freedom times R over two; Cp follows by adding R.
Gamma = Cp/Cv comes out 5/3 for monatomic and 7/5 for diatomic gases, matching measurement.

concepts.title: Mean Free Path
concepts.definition: Between collisions a molecule travels straight lines of random length; the average of these is the mean free path. It shrinks when molecules are bigger or the gas denser, and at atmospheric pressure it is a few hundred nanometres -- small, yet about a thousand times the molecular diameter.
concepts.key_idea: Mean free path is the typical clear runway between molecular collisions -- inversely tied to density and molecular size.
concepts.textbook_ref: keph205.txt lines 561-640 (section 12.7 mean free path, collision cross section, estimate at STP, collision frequency)
question_patterns: define mean free path of a gas molecule
in class 11 kinetic theory: on what factors does the mean free path depend
estimate the mean free path of air molecules at standard conditions
why is the mean free path much larger than the molecular diameter
how does mean free path change when the gas is compressed
relate collision frequency to mean free path and average speed

solution_steps.explain: A moving molecule sweeps a cylinder of diameter twice the molecular radius per unit path; collisions happen inside it.
The path length whose sweep cylinder holds one other molecule is the mean free path -- inversely proportional to number density.
At STP the mean free path of air molecules is a few hundred nanometres, giving collision rates of order a billion per second.
